faq.a: Ischemic microvascular palsy (common in diabetes) affects the peripheral motor fibers but spares the peripheral parasympathetic fibers that control pupil size.
faq.q: Why does a third‑nerve palsy sometimes spare the pupil?

faq.a: Ask the patient to smile or raise eyebrows; peripheral palsy lowers the entire half‑face, while central palsy spares the forehead.
faq.q: What bedside test distinguishes a peripheral from a central facial palsy?

faq.a: No; early TB meningitis often shows normal CT. CSF analysis remains essential.
faq.q: Can a normal CT scan rule out TB meningitis?

exam: A 30‑year‑old with HIV presents with diplopia on right gaze – what is your next bedside test and why? — Perform lateral gaze test for VI palsy; if abnormal, assess pupil size to differentiate compressive vs ischemic cause.

A child from a malaria‑endemic area has a fixed, dilated pupil and absent corneal reflex – what does this indicate and what immediate action is required? — Suggests brain‑stem involvement; arrange urgent transfer for neuro‑imaging and airway protection.

You find an isolated left facial weakness sparing the forehead in a diabetic patient – how do you explain the pattern and what management steps follow? — Peripheral VII palsy from microvascular ischemia; start supportive eye care and monitor; steroids not indicated.

A patient with TB meningitis develops a new VI palsy after 2 weeks of therapy – what does this tell you about disease progression and treatment? — Indicates ongoing basal meningitis or hydrocephalus; repeat CSF analysis and consider adjunctive steroids or surgical CSF diversion.

During a bedside exam you note absent gag reflex but normal palate elevation – which nerves are involved and what are the likely causes in a low‑resource setting? — IX (glossopharyngeal) dysfunction; common causes include TB meningitis, cryptococcal meningitis, or local skull base infection.

You suspect a compressive third‑nerve lesion; which pupil finding would confirm it and what would you do if imaging is unavailable? — Non‑reactive, dilated pupil; start high‑dose steroids for possible cavernous sinus inflammation and arrange urgent transfer for imaging.

A patient on antiretroviral therapy presents with bilateral facial weakness and taste loss – which cranial nerves are affected and what differential diagnoses are most relevant? — VII bilateral involvement; consider HIV‑related Bell’s palsy, cryptococcal meningitis, or syphilis.

In a rural clinic you cannot perform MRI; a patient has signs of a lateral medullary syndrome – how do you confirm the diagnosis and manage? — Use bedside cranial‑nerve exam (hoarseness, dysphagia, loss of pain/temp on one side of face) plus CT to rule out bleed; start antiplatelet therapy and arrange transfer.
ai.title: Cranial Nerves Overview
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A systematic approach to the twelve cranial nerves helps clinicians localise lesions, interpret common tropical presentations, and plan urgent investigations and management in low‑resource settings.

b: I – Olfactory (smell)
II – Optic (vision)
III – Oculomotor (eye movements, pupil)
IV – Trochlear (superior oblique)
V – Trigeminal (face sensation, mastication)
VI – Abducens (lateral gaze)
VII – Facial (facial expression, taste)
VIII – Vestibulocochlear (hearing, balance)
IX – Glossopharyngeal (taste, gag)
X – Vagus (viscera, voice)
XI – Accessory (sternocleidomastoid, trapezius)
XII – Hypoglossal (tongue movement)
sections.p: The twelve cranial nerves arise from the brainstem or forebrain and carry motor, sensory or mixed information. Knowing the order (I‑XII) and primary function lets you map a patient’s deficits to a specific nerve or brain‑stem level.

b: Motor: eye movements (III, IV, VI), facial smile (VII), tongue protrusion (XII).
Sensory: corneal reflex (V‑VII), gag (IX‑X), taste on anterior 2/3 (VII) and posterior 1/3 (IX).
Reflexes: jaw‑jerk (V), gag (IX‑X).
sections.p: Clinical localisation follows a stepwise exam: inspection → motor → sensory → reflexes → special tests. In low‑resource hospitals, bedside tests replace imaging when possible.

b: TB meningitis – early VI palsy, later III‑VI palsies, altered consciousness.
Neurosyphilis – III palsy with pupil sparing, tabes dorsalis affecting V.
HIV‑related cryptococcal meningitis – VI palsy, papilledema (II).
Malaria cerebral – diffuse cranial‑nerve dysfunction, especially VI.
Herbal neurotoxins – isolated VII palsy with taste loss.
sections.p: Common tropical conditions produce characteristic cranial‑nerve patterns. Recognising these patterns guides urgent treatment and avoids missing life‑threatening brain‑stem involvement.

t.b: Is there mass effect or hydrocephalus? → guides need for neurosurgical referral.
Opening pressure and CSF analysis for TB, cryptococcus, syphilis. If LP unsafe, treat empirically for TB meningitis.
Is the pupil reactive? → differentiates compressive III palsy (non‑reactive) from ischemic (reactive).

b: Always start with a systematic cranial‑nerve exam; missing one nerve loses marks.
Link a focal deficit to the neuro‑anatomical level before jumping to a diagnosis.
In resource‑limited settings, describe what you would do if CT or MRI were unavailable.
sections.p: Examiners test your ability to integrate history, exam and limited investigations to reach a working diagnosis and immediate plan.

b: Confusing a peripheral VII palsy (Bell’s palsy) with central facial weakness (stroke).
Relying on absent corneal reflex alone to diagnose V lesion – must assess sensation and jaw‑jerk.
Assuming normal pupil rules out serious III palsy – compressive lesions may have delayed dilation.
sections.p: Students often list nerves without clinical context or assume a single test can confirm a diagnosis.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly progressive bilateral VI palsy – risk of brain‑stem herniation
Sudden loss of consciousness with fixed dilated pupils – possible posterior fossa bleed
Severe dysphagia with aspiration in TB meningitis – airway protection needed
